extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, economists, patent scholars, IP policymakers, and patent professionals interested in empirical analysis of continuation practice in the U.S. patent system
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical analysis of firms' use of continuation procedures (CAP, CIP, divisional) in U.S. utility patenting (priority years 1981–2000; issues through 2004), linking continuation incidence to patent, assignee, and technology characteristics and to policy changes (1995 patent-term change; 1999 publication rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of continuations (CAP, CIP, Division)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three types of 'continuations': the Continuation Application (CAP), the Continuation-In-Part (CIP), and the Division. The CAP discloses the identical invention claimed in the prior parent non-provisional application. The CIP includes a substantial portion or all of the parent application and adds matter not disclosed in that application. A Division/divisional application is filed when the original application contains more than one independent invention and the applicant elects one invention for continued examination while pursuing the others in divisional applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal bases: Continuation and CIP authorized under 35 U.S.C. §120; Divisions under 35 U.S.C. §121. CAP must not introduce 'new matter' relative to the parent; CIP only gets the parent's priority date for subject matter that was disclosed in the parent. Divisional can benefit from the parent's filing date only if it discloses and claims material present in the parent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions to claim priority under 35 U.S.C. §120
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. §120, a later application is entitled to adopt the filing date of a 'parent' application when (1) both applications disclose the same invention; (2) both applications are filed by the same inventor; (3) both applications are simultaneously co-pending; (4) the earlier application meets the disclosure requirements of 35 U.S.C. §112; and (5) the later application contains a specific reference to the earlier application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court precedents (e.g., Sampson v. Ampex Corp. (1971)) and CCPA/Patent Office practice interpret these conditions; failure to meet them can deny priority benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendency (lag between priority and issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pendency is the delay (years) between the priority (first application) date and the patent issue date. Ordinary (non-continuation) patents average ~2.2 years pendency; continued patents average ~4.4 years (s.d. 2.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer pendency for continuations introduces truncation bias when analyzing issued patents by issue year; use priority year/date to avoid biased inferences about trends. Pendency distributions: many continuation patents issue within 4–8 years but a nontrivial share take much longer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of claims defines the formal scope of the patent and, controlling for technology, is correlated with economic value; litigated patents tend to have more claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims data were used for patents granted between 1981 and 1997 in this study. CIPs produce patents with more claims (e.g., ~26% more than ordinary patents), reflecting use to bring in additional material. Use number of claims as a proxy for breadth/value, controlling for technology class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backward citations (count)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of prior patents cited by a patent (applicant- and examiner-inserted), used to reveal technological lineage and crowdedness of the inventive area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high count of backward citations to other entities indicates operation in a crowded area; patents resulting from continuations contain higher numbers of backward citations on average. From 2001 the PTO distinguishes examiner- vs applicant-inserted citations—applicant-inserted citations are consistent with applicants strengthening applications via continuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share of backward self-citations
rubrics_metrics.description: The fraction of backward citations that cite patents assigned to the same assignee (self-cites).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High self-citation share suggests the patent builds on the assignee's prior work rather than competitor prior art; CIPs show significantly higher backward self-citation shares, consistent with building on the firm's prior inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality (technology-class dispersion of backward citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Herfindahl index measuring the concentration/dispersion of backward citations across technology classes: 0 when all backward citations are to a single class (low originality) and 1 for perfect dispersion (high originality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher dispersion (higher originality index) suggests the invention draws on a broader spectrum of prior art and may be more 'original.' Continued patents have higher average dispersion, robust to controls for number of backward citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward citations (fcites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations made to a patent by subsequent patents; commonly used as indicators of technological importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reduce truncation bias, restrict forward citations to those appearing within a fixed window (e.g., four years after issue) when comparing patents across vintages. CIPs receive higher 4-year forward citations on average, indicating higher technological importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent renewal behavior (4-, 8-, 12-year renewals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patentholder pays renewal fees at statutory intervals (4, 8, 12 years after grant), used as an indicator of private value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners renew only when expected value exceeds maintenance costs; 4-year nonrenewal rates are used as a short-run private-value measure. CIPs are less likely to expire after 4 years, suggesting higher private value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant vs examiner inserted citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between citations added by applicants and those inserted by examiners (reported on the patent wrapper starting in 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A higher share of applicant-inserted citations in continuation patents suggests applicants actively shape the disclosure/claims through continuations. Continued patents in the sample had smaller shares of examiner-inserted citations compared to ordinary patents (20% vs 55% in one comparison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-of-continuation categories and counts (CAP/CIP/Division/Combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize patents as resulting from CAP, CIP, Division, Combination (multiple types) or ordinary (no continuation), and compute frequencies by priority year and technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For 1981–2000 priority years in this dataset, ~29% of corporate-assigned patents had at least one continuation; CAPs were the most common followed by CIPs and Divisions. Combination continuations are heterogeneous and often excluded from focused analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology classification effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign patents to technology classes (NBER aggregation: 36 subcategories, aggregated to 6 main categories) and analyze continuation incidence and type by technology sector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuation patterns vary by field: Drugs & Medicine and Chemicals heavily use CIPs and combinations (high continuation share); Computers & Communications have a higher share of CAPs; semiconductors show high divisional propensity. Control for technology to avoid confounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee (firm) characteristics influencing continuation propensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable firm attributes used as predictors: patenting intensity, R&D intensity, capital intensity, firm size (employment), firm age, technology share/time in a domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link patents to Compustat firms via NBER correspondence file. Publicly listed firms differ from private firms in continuation use (e.g., in-sample public firms more likely to have CAPs & Divisions, less likely CIPs). Include these controls and interactions in regression models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patenting intensity (lnPATINT) and R&D intensity (lnRDINT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuous measures of a firm's patenting and R&D intensity used in regressions (log-transformed), often interacted to capture heterogeneous effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interactions (lnRDINT * lnPATINT) and with patent-quality (fcites) are used to test how firm strategy and patent value jointly affect continuation choices; interpret coefficients in the context of interaction terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-quality proxy interactions (fcites * firm attributes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interaction variables combining forward citations (fcites) with firm intensity measures (e.g., FCITES*lnRDINT*lnPATINT) to test whether higher-quality patents by certain firm types are more/less likely to be continued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such interactions in multinomial/probit models to test whether the relationship between patent quality and continuation choice changed after policy reforms (e.g., 1995 law). Include technology and application-vintage fixed effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of policy changes (1995 patent-term change; 1999 publication rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy reforms: 1995 changed patent term from 17 years from issue to 20 years from application date; 1999 mandated publication of most applications after 18 months (with opt-out for US-only filings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1995 reduced incentives for 'submarine' strategies by making extended pendency trade off against lost term; 1999 publication reduced secrecy benefits but did not eliminate strategic uses (applicants can still alter claims in continuations). Empirically test pre/post changes and analyze shifts in continuation composition (e.g., reduced overall use; CAPs shifted toward less-important patents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for Continued Examination (RCE) as prosecution option
rubrics_metrics.description: A procedural option after 'final rejection' allowing the applicant another round of examination while preserving priority date; treated like a new application but often assigned to the same examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RCEs differ procedurally from continuations but serve similar prosecution-extension purposes; consider RCE filings (and examiner reassignment exceptions) when characterizing prosecution strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truncation and vintage bias controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytical consideration that more recent priority/application years will have unobserved continuation/issue outcomes because of long pendency; use priority-year grouping, restrict samples, and use fixed windows for citation counts to mitigate bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit analysis to patents with priority years where sufficient issue data exist (e.g., 1981–2000 priority years, issues through 2004). Restrict forward citations to a 4-year post-issue window and use priority-year or application-period dummies to control for vintage effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluding/handling heterogeneous categories (Divisions, Combinations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisions and Combination continuations are heterogeneous: Divisions often result from PTO restriction requirements (less strategic), Combination patents involve multiple continuation types and mixed motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude Divisions and Combinations from some analyses focusing on strategic applicant-driven continuation behavior (CAP and CIP), or treat them separately because their interpretation differs.
